newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Deal in sight on EU fishing curbs.
newsitem.headline: Deal in sight on EU fishing curbs.

text.p: Agreement is within reach next week on controversial plans for sharp cuts in fish catches over the next three years to protect endangered stocks, European Union officials and diplomats said on Friday.

They said a large majority of member states, with the notable exception of Britain, has welcomed a compromise of the Dutch EU Presidency softening cuts proposed by EU Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino and making them more flexible.
"Most member states feel the time is now ripe for a decision," said a diplomat from a major fishing nation.

But the diplomat warned that there was still much haggling ahead at the two-day meeting, starting in Luxembourg on Monday, over the rate and shape of the cuts, size of exempted small fishing vessels and fleet renewal rules.

Strong opposition is expected from Britain's Conservative government, fighting an uphill battle for re-election on May 1. It has insisted that the EU must first solve the problem of "quota hoppers" - vessels from one EU state which register in another to take part of its quota.
Around 20 percent of the British national fish quota is now allocated to 150 foreign, mainly Spanish and Dutch, vessels registered under the British flag.
The issue is being discussed separately as part of a review of the EU Treaty, due to be completed in June, to prepare for the membership of central and east European countries.
Britain risks being outvoted as the European Commission has signalled it could reluctantly accept the views of the majority of member states, diplomats said.
Unanimity would otherwise have been required to overturn the Commission's original proposal for fleet capacity cuts of up to 40 percent over six years to the end of 2002.
Under the Dutch compromise, cuts of 30 percent and 20 percent would be made for endangered and overfished stocks.
"The Commission would have preferred something stronger like our original proposal but we can go along with it," Fisheries spokesman Filippo di Robilant said.
Member states would choose whether to cut fish catches by laying up vessels, reducing fishing effort -- time spent hunting stocks in targeted areas with specified gear -- or a combination of both.
But there will still be a lot of haggling over the size of the cuts which most states still think are too swingeing.
EU countries were given an extra four months to agree on a new fishing reduction programme after failing to meet an end- December deadline.
Failure to agree next week would result in the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars of aid annually for fishing communities to adjust to the changes, Di Robilant warned.
